articles.title: Twenty-Six Defense unveils new soldier-worn tech
articles.snippet: The defense firm formerly known as Elbit America introduced Primex, a headset designed with night vision and augmented reality capabilities.
articles.full_text:
The company that previously operated as Elbit Systems’ American subsidiary made its AUSA expo debut this week as Twenty-Six Defense.
Under the new brand, the Texas-based defense firm debuted Primex, a lightweight wearable meant to provide soldiers with night-vision capabilities and augmented reality so they can “maintain awareness without distraction or cognitive overload.”
For the design, Twenty-Six Defense said it engineered Primex for sustained operational use by equipping it with “the lightest head-borne load and near-neutral center of gravity.”
The company explained Primex uses low-light sensors, thermal imagery, and real-time processing to produce an ultra-low-latency digital perception that enables operators to better interpret the surrounding area even amid challenging environmental conditions.
What separates Primex from other advanced lightweight heads-up display units for operators, according to Twenty-Six Defense, is that its design was built on mature technologies that have already been fielded.
The company said it already produces AN/PSQ-44 Enhanced Night Vision Goggles, which contain features that allow for rapid target acquisition and augment reality to enhance visual clarity.
In August, Ernie Basic, Twenty-Six Defense’s senior director of research and development, explained how his company was developing equipment for the Soldier Borne Mission Command, a project to deliver augmented reality wearables to soldiers.
He said the technology combines fighter-pilot displays with night-vision systems, so soldiers get “the full operational picture.”
“You are not only seeing what is in front of you. You can leverage a feed coming from a drone or from other assets,” he said. “You can start seeing what is going on behind a house or another structure, cue a squad to a different location, and continuously update them.”
In addition to Primex, Twenty-Six Defense showcased defensive weapons and equipment like the XM1168 mobile 120mm mortar system, Autonomous Relocatable Surveillance Tower and SkyStriker Block 4E.
Daniel Terrill is a contributor to Military Times. He’s been reporting on military issues, the gun industry, and the outdoors for nearly two decades. Although writing is his passion, he’s been a Marine, police officer, and, perhaps the most dangerous job of his career, a substitute teacher.

articles.title: Italy eyes MBDA armaments for new Italo-Turkish drone
articles.snippet: The Italian air force is due to acquire six of the drones, which are derived from Baykar’s TB-3 and are being assembled in Italy by LBA Systems.
articles.full_text:
ROME — Italy is holding tests with MBDA to mount the European firm’s armaments on the new Astore Levante drone being built by Turkey’s Baykar and Italy’s Leonardo, the head of the Italian air force has said.
The Italian air force is due to acquire six of the drones, which are derived from Baykar’s TB-3 and are being assembled in Italy by LBA Systems, a joint venture between Baykar and Leonardo.
The Astore Levante is due to carry Leonardo sensors, but at its unveiling at the Farnborough air show in July it was presented alongside Turkish armaments, including Roketsan’s MAM family of guided bombs and Baykar’s KEMANKES-1 mini cruise missile.
Speaking in Rome on Monday, Italian air force chief Gen. Antonio Conserva said he was not ruling out other suppliers of armaments. “At the moment we have not made choices, the natural armament is Turkish but we also have activities with MBDA and small Italian industrial groups,” he said.
Conserva confirmed the new drone was set to be certified by the end of 2026 or in early 2027. European certification is deemed a prerequisite for selling the drone in Europe.
Mounting European arms will also boost sales efforts in Europe. The Italian air force will initially order three systems, each containing two drones, but Conserva said, “We will see if we go on to expand the capability.”
The Astore Levant will replace the Predator MQ1 flown by the air force, Conserva added. As well as being flown on ISR missions and providing armed support for troops, the drones will also be used for training drone pilots, he said.
Before the launch in July of the Astore Levante, the Italian navy said in April it was eyeing the TB-3 as a carrier-borne drone to fly off its Cavour carrier, which also hosts Italy’s F-35Bs.
The TB-3 is already in service on board the Turkish amphibious assault ship TCG Anadolu. Another TB-3 customer, Indonesia, is expected to base the drone on the Garibaldi, a carrier it has purchased from Italy.
Conserva spoke to reporters on Monday at a conference at the HQ of the Italian air force in Rome which gathered air force and industry officials to discuss the future of warfare.
Asked by Defense News about the prospect of Germany possibly joining the GCAP sixth generation fighter program set up by Italy, Japan and the UK, Conserva said he was in favor.
“We are talking about a strategic partner,” he said.
“We would need to find a political and industrial deal. Germany is a great country. We have already collaborated with them on the Tornado which will retire next year, and the Eurofighter which is the backbone of our national defense and deterrence. Whatever emerges I will view favorably,” he added.
Tom Kington is the Italy correspondent for Defense News.

articles.title: US Army creates robotics technician job to focus on drone warfare
articles.snippet: As experts in autonomous warfare, U.S. Army robotics technicians will advise commanders on how best to deploy autonomous systems during operations.
articles.full_text:
The U.S. Army kickstarted a military occupational specialty focusing on robotics and unmanned systems with an induction ceremony this month at the U.S. Army John F. Kennedy Special Warfare Center and School.
During the ceremony, 10 warrant officers were formally introduced as 390A robotics technicians. They will now serve as subject-matter experts on all aspects of using robotic and autonomous systems, including programming, building and repairing them, plus integrating them into combat.
The 390A inauguration is the result of a lengthy process that has been in the works since 2024, when U.S. Army Special Operations Command announced its aim to train experts in using autonomous systems.
The Army deemed it necessary to introduce robotics as a separate specialization to avoid overburdening special warfare operators with having to master an additional, highly complex skill set, in addition to their existing knowledge.
“What we’ve determined is it cannot be an additional task or an additional hat for someone on the ODA,” Chief Warrant Officer 5 Jerry Brown, command chief warrant officer for 1st Special Forces Command (Airborne), said in a release, adding that the new specialists will be able to leverage their specific field of knowledge within robotics to help the force as a whole.
The new 390A technicians will be assigned to tactical formations at the brigade and group level. As experts in autonomous warfare, they will advise commanders on how best to deploy autonomous systems during operations.
They will also be required to think quickly in the field to instantly propose solutions to any problems that may arise with robotics in the field, and to use their expertise to come up with innovative ways of using drones to reach objectives.
To prepare them for this role, 390A candidates are required to complete a 19-week course, where they must build drones from scratch that do not require GPS or radio frequencies to navigate.
The Army stated in a release that robotic systems assembled during the course will rely primarily on artificial intelligence and machine learning to navigate to targets.
Fiber optic cables also provide a way for drones to reach targets while being invulnerable to external signal interference, such as jamming. Known as “tethered drones,” cable-linked unmanned aircraft systems can use artificial intelligence for targeting and navigation while having a direct physical connection to their operator.
At the time of publication, the Army had not responded to questions about whether 390A candidates would be learning to build and field tethered drones.
“The Army is implementing changes in force structures, adding a multi-domain task force equipped with autonomous long-range fires,” Gen. Christopher LaNeve, Vice Chief of Staff of the Army, said in a statement.
“These technical experts will help command teams understand integration across the force. We are scaling this across the Army.”
Zita Ballinger Fletcher previously served as editor of Military History Quarterly and Vietnam magazines and as the historian of the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration. She holds an M.A. with distinction in military history.

articles.title: Lockheed’s New PAC-3 Edge interceptor aims for agility
articles.snippet: The defense giant unveiled the PAC-3 Edge this Friday and debuted it at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting on Monday.
articles.full_text:
The latest iteration of Lockheed Martin’s PAC-3 family of missile interceptors is designed to bring extreme agility to bear against a diverse array of missile threats, Defense News learned.
The defense giant unveiled the PAC-3 Edge this Friday and debuted it at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington, D.C., today.
“This missile is capable of being launched from the traditional M903 launcher. It’s capable of being launched from the containerized launchers that are being sought after domestically and internationally, as well as our HIMARS FLEX, which is the offense and defense configuration of our traditional HIMARS vehicle,” Jason Reynolds, vice president and general manager of Lockheed Martin Missiles and Fire Control Integrated Air and Missile Defense, told Defense News.
Lockheed in January announced a seven-year framework agreement to increase annual PAC-3 interceptor production from approximately 600 to 2,000.
Designed to defend against hypersonic and advanced missile threats, the unveiling of the PAC-3 Edge comes as the U.S. military’s reliance on costly interceptors against cheap munitions, particularly those deployed by Iran during Operation Epic Fury, has come under increased scrutiny over the past eight months.
The new PAC-3 Edge missile builds on the foundations of the PAC-3 MSE, Lockheed’s baseline missile, and pushes its abilities farther.
The Edge system is longer and features a larger diameter, increasing its range.
“It also goes higher in altitude and has more agility. It has attitude control motors, which are located near the front of the missile and basically divert the missile in flight,” Reynolds explained. “This has additional attitude control motors that give it additional agility.”
While the PAC-3 MSE uses a two-pulse solid rocket motor to speedily approach moving targets, the new system has multi-pulse motor designed by Northrop Grumman.
“It has a third pulse to the motor, so that means the motor will fire three times during its flight, giving it additional agility to kill the target,” Reynolds said.
The weapon is designed not only for unprecedented maneuverability but to be easily integrated with both present and future missile defense networks. It is compatible with Northrop’s Integrated Battle Command System, or IBCS, a command-and-control network the Army uses to mesh air and missile defense sensors into a central hub.
The company intends to begin testing the PAC-3 Edge in 2027 and have it ready to deploy by 2031, although Lockheed aims to have it ready earlier, Reynolds added.
“The U.S. Army’s timeline is 2031. We, Lockheed Martin, are trying to pull that in and deliver this capability sooner, so around the turn of the decade,” he said.
Zita Ballinger Fletcher previously served as editor of Military History Quarterly and Vietnam magazines and as the historian of the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration. She holds an M.A. with distinction in military history.

articles.title: Sikorsky packs 4 Nomad drones into a single shipping container
articles.snippet: Nomad 100 fast pack fits four aircraft, mission-command software, power, communications and sustainment equipment inside one standard shipping container.
articles.full_text:
Sikorsky on Monday introduced a containerized kit that packs four of its Nomad 100 drones and the gear needed to fly them into a single shipping container. The announcement came as the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting opened in Washington.
The Nomad 100 fast pack fits four aircraft, mission-command software, power, communications and sustainment equipment inside one standard 20-foot shipping container, the company said in a release.
In its planned configuration, two of the aircraft can be mission ready in under 15 minutes, and the other two available within four to six hours, according to Sikorsky.
The system is designed to launch without a runway from sites such as naval vessels, tactical vehicle staging areas and improvised landing zones. After a mission, crews can repack the container, load it onto a compatible vehicle and move it to a new site.
Depending on how a customer configures it, the kit could support intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance and targeting missions, as well as light attack and contested logistics, the company said.
Sikorsky said the U.S. military needs to rapidly expand its inventory of autonomous aircraft with compact systems that can be deployed, sustained and moved quickly in contested environments.
“By packaging aircraft, mission command, communications, power and sustainment into a single containerized system, we are making it easier to move, employ and reposition VTOL UAS capability with urgency and flexibility,” Rich Benton, Sikorsky’s vice president and general manager, said in the release.
The Nomad 100 has an 18-foot wingspan and is a Group 3 drone under the Defense Department’s classification system. It uses Sikorsky’s rotor blown wing design, which pairs a helicopter’s vertical lift and hover with the speed, range and endurance of a fixed-wing aircraft, and it flies with the company’s MATRIX autonomy software.
The company has not released the Nomad 100’s payload, range or endurance.
Sikorsky developed the aircraft with funding from the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, or DARPA, under its Early VTOL Aircraft Demonstration program, known as EVADE.
In July, Sikorsky said it had finished initial ground and flight testing of the Nomad 100 and would next put the drone through an intensive flight test campaign at a government facility. The company said DARPA chose MATRIX as the autonomy system for all five aircraft in the EVADE program.
Sikorsky introduced the Nomad family in October 2025, after an extended flight test of a smaller prototype, the Nomad 50, with a 10.3-foot wingspan.
Monday’s release did not say whether a fast pack has been built, or whether any military service has ordered or is evaluating one.
Michael Scanlon is a defense journalist covering air and space warfare. A former U.S. Air Force A-10 crew chief, he has supported land and sea programs for the U.S. Army, Navy, Marine Corps and Coast Guard.

articles.title: 3 US soldiers awarded Purple Hearts after March missile attack on Saudi Arabia base
articles.snippet: Sgt. Xavier Jones, SSgt. Kalob Mitchell and Spc. Nicholas Cabo were awarded Purple Hearts after a missile attack on Prince Sultan Air Base, Saudi Arabia.
articles.full_text:
Three U.S. soldiers were awarded Purple Hearts for their efforts assisting fellow service members despite their own injuries after a missile attack hit their air base during Operation Epic Fury.
On March 27, when a missile hit Prince Sultan Air Base in Al Kharj, Saudi Arabia, Staff Sgt. Kalob Mitchell, Spc. Nicholas Cabo and Sgt. Xavier Jones, all with the 6th Battalion, 56th Air Defense Artillery Regiment, 1st Cavalry Division Artillery, sprang into action.
A 550-pound ballistic missile exploded yards from a bunker on base, filling it with dust and debris.
“We’re sitting there talking, and then all of a sudden, we didn’t hear anything, no sound at all. Everything went black, so we were hit,” Mitchell said in a recent release.
While expecting just another missile warning, the soldiers were thrown from their position and slammed against the opposing interior wall, forcing all three to lose consciousness. They had their initial medical evaluation later that day at the Role 2 Medical Facility on base.
“Woke up, checked on them. They were good. At that time, we heard screams from the opposite side of the bunker. Two Soldiers, I’m not too sure who they were, who had significant injuries; ran over there, applied tourniquets, T Triple C (Tactical Combat Casualty Care), everything,” Mitchell recounted.
Mitchell, Cabo and Jones applied a tourniquet to a severely wounded soldier, treated another with a neck injury and helped keep a disoriented soldier safe until it was safe to evacuate the bunker, per the release.
Despite their own injuries, the trio continued to assist others, carrying others out to an ambulance and helping a soldier whose leg was severely damaged, speculating that the soldier could have lost their life if not for the group.
Capt. Tyler Ritter, commander of 6-56 ADAR, 1st Cav. DIVARTY, received messages from the injured soldier saying, “Sir, your Soldiers saved my life. I thank God every day that these gentlemen survived. Their actions brought great credit upon the 6-56 Air Defense Artillery Regiment, 1st Cavalry Division and III Armored Corps. These Soldiers are my heroes. May God bless them.”
Mitchell, Cabo and Jones’ service, described as the “ultimate description of what we mean when we talk about warfighting, readiness, grit and taking care of our Soldiers,” earned them each a Purple Heart during an Oct. 1 ceremony at the III Armored Corps headquarters building at Fort Hood, Texas.
“So honestly, it’s kind of cool,” Jones said in the release. “I don’t think any of us was like going for a Purple Heart because it actually sucked. Like that situation was horrible … When I saw it on my STP (Soldier Talent Profile), I was like, man, I never would have thought I would have got a Purple Heart. I never thought I was going to see anything like we saw.”
Cristina Stassis is a reporter covering stories surrounding the defense industry, national security, military/veteran affairs and more. She previously worked as an editorial fellow for Defense News in 2024 where she assisted the newsroom in breaking news across Sightline Media Group.

articles.title: Ukraine is building a patchwork antiballistic defense, one stopgap at a time
articles.snippet: Kyiv is relying on stockpile transfers, Patriot and Aster licenses and the Freyja interceptor to survive the winter — but time is running short.
articles.full_text:
KYIV, Ukraine — Ukraine is scrambling to secure enough Patriot interceptors to stop Russian ballistic missiles this winter, piecing together allied stockpile transfers, new production agreements and a homegrown interceptor program as quickly as possible before the cold sets in.
The push comes as the world runs short on the weapons Ukraine needs most. U.S. forces in Europe face a “beyond critical” shortage of Patriot interceptors after stocks were moved to the Middle East for the Iran war, a NATO official said in August.
Ukraine is also bracing for another winter of Russian strikes on its energy grid, a campaign that increasingly relies on jet-powered Shahed drones too fast for most of the cheap interceptor drones Ukraine has used to stop older models.
“Russia uses almost only jet-powered Shaheds to attack Kyiv because the interceptors that we were using in the past against older generations of drones had an interception rate of around 90%,” a manager at Ukrainian interceptor developer Grim Tech told Defense News last month.
The faster drones force Ukraine to expend scarce and expensive missiles just as it tries to conserve Patriot ammunition for ballistic threats — the only reliable option against Russia’s even harder-to-stop ballistic missiles, according to Ukrainian officials.
“Ballistic missiles are especially difficult to deal with,” President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said after a massive aerial barrage on Wednesday night saw Russia fire 70 missiles, many of them ballistic, and waves of Shahed drones at Kyiv and 12 other regions.
Soldiers downed 39 of the 48 cruise missiles but only five ballistic missiles, according to Ukraine’s air force. At least 32 people were killed in the attacks, and over 100 were injured, Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram.
Civilian casualties in Ukraine have risen monthly throughout most of 2026. U.N. monitors verified 372 civilians killed and 2,349 injured in August, second only to July, with long-range missiles and drones causing 47% of the toll.
Kyiv is assembling a patchwork of antiballistic air defense solutions, each piece on a different clock: Rounds transferred from allied stocks for this winter, imported systems and licensed production that will begin to matter over the next several years, and Freyja, a Ukrainian-European interceptor still in development.
Stockpile swaps
The fastest fix depends on allies sharing existing stockpiles, a request Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara put forward at his first Ukraine Defense Contact Group meeting with allies on Sept. 8.
Kyiv has signed contracts for roughly 1,000 Patriot missiles in recent months, but most will not ship for years, Khmara said.
He asked partners for 300 interceptors from their stockpiles now, offering newer missiles from those contracts as replacements.
“The situation with ballistics is much more difficult. And that difficulty is precisely down to the lack of Patriot missiles,” he told allies.
Germany answered Khmara’s call by promising an undisclosed number of PAC-2 interceptors from Bundeswehr stocks.
Britain committed £100 million through NATO’s Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) for Patriot missiles and other air-defense equipment intended to arrive before winter, according to the British government.
But the United States did not include Patriot missiles in the nearly $400 million in expiring Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative money it moved to obligate before the fiscal year ended, a source familiar with the package told Reuters.
Surging production of existing antiballistic interceptors
“Ukraine is ready not only to produce ballistic missile interceptors for its own needs, but also to strengthen the United States and its allies through joint production,” Zelenskyy wrote on X after a recent meeting with a U.S. congressional delegation in Kyiv.
Both Europe and the U.S. are in talks with Ukraine to begin ramping up joint manufacturing initiatives for both the Patriot missile system and the Franco-Italian Aster 30.
Zelenskyy said Sept. 25 that U.S. President Donald Trump made a final political decision to grant Ukraine licenses to produce Patriot missiles. But Washington and manufacturers have not publicly identified the variant, Ukraine’s workshare, production site or first-delivery date.
Lockheed Martin said it aims to raise its own annual PAC-3 MSE capacity from roughly 600 missiles to 2,000 by 2030, while a $14.7 billion Boeing contract would triple production of the interceptor’s seeker.
Germany is scheduled to begin PAC-2 GEM-T production, and Berlin has separately asked Washington and Lockheed Martin to permit PAC-3 MSE production in Germany, but that proposal remains unresolved.
France and Italy agreed in a joint declaration in July to authorize licensed production of Aster 30 interceptors in Ukraine before the end of 2026, along with providing Kyiv with four SAMP/T NG systems — becoming their first combat user.
France also committed two interim SAMP/T complexes, a GF300 radar before year’s end and progressive SAMP/T NG deployment beginning in 2027.
The sovereignty bet: Freyja
Ukraine and Europe are looking to a new weapon called “Frejya” as a longer-term solution.
Freyja is a Ukrainian-designed ballistic interceptor built around Fire Point’s FP-7.X missile, including an interceptor, launcher, radar and command-and-control network.
It’s priced at roughly $1 million per round, about one-quarter of the cost of a PAC-3 MSE, and designed to plug into NATO-standard radars and command posts already in the field.
The FP-7.X flew for the first time in early June and is built to kill ballistic targets at roughly 15 miles up using a high-explosive fragmentation warhead rather than the PAC-3’s hit-to-kill collision — which may come in later versions — at a target price of approximately $700,000 per interceptor, or roughly one-fifth the price of a PAC-3.
The company says it will build three interceptors a day starting in August. Zelenskyy wants the system up and running within a year, and the coalition is targeting its first real ballistic intercept for the end of 2027.
Zelenskyy launched the initiative with nine European countries in Paris in July — and the effort is still growing.
Poland joined the group on Sept. 17, a week after Canadian PM Mark Carney told Zelenskyy that Ottawa would contribute its technologies to Freyja along with providing Kyiv with a broader package that includes C$350 million in interceptors.
The EU is separately weighing direct funding for the program on top of national contributions, according to Militarnyi.
Katie Livingstone is the Ukraine correspondent for Defense News and Military Times. Based in Kyiv, she has covered Russia's full-scale invasion since its first days. She is a former Fulbright fellow whose award-winning work has appeared in outlets across Europe and the U.S.

articles.title: ‘Noticeable shift in warfare’: US Army under secretary on the lessons of modern combat
articles.snippet: U.S. Army innovation and acquisition is entering unprecedented territory. Army Under Secretary Mike Obadal (left) is at the center of these efforts.
articles.full_text:
The U.S. Army is entering unprecedented territory.
Demand for exquisite munitions has skyrocketed as conflicts in Iran and Ukraine — and an ever-tense Indo-Pacific — continue to redefine stockpile demand.
So, too, has there developed an insatiable market for cheap systems and interceptors capable of balancing scales that, in regions like the Middle East, have been encumbered by cost-per-kill ratios as lopsided as 114-1 — in the case of a PAC-3 interceptor versus a Shahed-136 drone.
If that weren’t enough to consider, there’s the lightning-quick speed of AI integration and unmanned systems into formations, and the reality of having to rethink a simple concept — hiding — that was seldom given a second thought due to the total air superiority of the Global War on Terror.
Such frenzied developments, meanwhile, come against a backdrop of new Pentagon policy that aims to eliminate the antiquated red tape of the acquisition process and speed development to the battlefield.
A daunting cluster of problems to solve, no doubt. But if encountering such a catalog of to-dos is stress-inducing, one would not know it when speaking to U.S. Army Under Secretary Mike Obadal, who finds himself at the center of many of these discussions.
From his office and out on the trail, Obadal oversees the service’s business operations, acquisition strategy, and manpower and personnel systems, among myriad other duties.
Obadal assumed the position after a stint in the private sector, which followed a military career that included time as a Special Operations officer, the status of Master Army Aviator and qualifications in nine different aircraft.
Obadal spoke to Military Times about how he and the Army are approaching these seismic shifts in warfighting philosophy, and how this year’s AUSA exposition reflects the blistering pace of innovation that catalyzes them.
There are many examples of individuals without military experience working in consequential positions within the Pentagon. You are not one. How has your military experience shaped how you approach this role?
What I try very hard to do is not let my experience drive the way I do things. I want it to inform the way I do things, whether that’s my experience working with the interagency and seeing how other executive branch agencies operate, my experience in the conventional military or in other parts of the military, doing joint work, working with partners and allies or going out into corporate America.
I don’t want any one of those things to be the driver of how I make decisions and conduct myself in the business of the Army, but I do want all of it to come together and inform it.
So, it’s certainly very helpful for me when I talk to soldiers or when I look at programs or weapon systems.
The biggest thing it helps me with is understanding that there’s no single weapon system that operates by itself anywhere. They are all part of a joint force, and within that, you have a maneuver Army that is reliant — tanks are reliant on infantry, infantry is reliant on fires, all of it is reliant on aviation, medical and logistics.
All those components work together as a chain, and you have to make sure every link in the chain is as strong as possible.
That’s one of the biggest things that I take away from being in the military: an understanding that all of these things have to work in synergy, and there are no easy solutions.
We continue to watch the conflicts in Ukraine and Iran unfold. What do you expect to see at an event like AUSA that reflects what America has learned from them?
If you walk around the hall at AUSA, it’ll give you a good indication of the Army’s priorities. Our priorities are reflected in what we’re procuring.
Going back several years, when we were in the Middle East and we first saw adversary drones — counter-drone systems became a really important topic. It kind of started in the special operations and then expanded into the larger Army.
Ukraine has not just reinforced that counter-UAS is a critical part of operations today; it’s cemented it.
So, if you walk around AUSA, you’re going to see an immense number of not only drones but also counter-UAS. That’s a reflection of the procurement and the budget, not just in the Army but in the Pentagon.
That’s number one. Number two is software. Being able to see, sense and integrate to understand what your positional advantage is, and understand the adversary and their vulnerabilities.
That’s just military operations, but today it’s looking at how we apply the best sensors and best software to bring all of that together to give decision advantage to our commanders.
The third one is fires, and when you look at current conflicts, the importance of long-range precision fires is highlighted.
So, what you’ll also see at the conference is a reflection of our investment portfolio in our magazine depth, but also the variety of munitions.
Expanding out the optionality that commanders have beyond just one or two exquisite munitions, with everything from longer-range artillery, one-way attack and loitering munitions, up into our higher-end missiles.
All of those represent our fires portfolio, but that’s just for offensive operations. When we get into the defensive side, we’ll be seeing everything from ballistic missiles down to Group One drones.
If you look at those three areas — drones and counter-UAS; software and sensors; and the fires portfolio — and were to roll back the clock to AUSA 10 years ago, the difference is remarkable.
At that time, the focus was very vehicle-centric, armor-centric, pieces of kit for individual soldiers. All of those things are important and are continuing to advance, but these newer investment areas represent a noticeable shift in warfare.
These conflicts are obviously influencing the speed of acquisition. But that process includes an emphasis on both cost-friendly and exquisite munition stockpiles. What is the best balance to ensure success?
The conflicts are definitely influencing and accelerating the way the Army — and certainly the broader Department — are innovating, prototyping, procuring and then fielding different capabilities.
If you were to roll back a decade or even less, you would see very traditional models that go from experimentation into writing an initial requirement document, then into prototyping, then selection, then low-rate production and then finally into fielding and high-rate production.
That’s years long. That process is very deliberate, and it built our military to where it is today, which is still the most dominant, but with a number of vulnerabilities because of technical innovation in the commercial market that adversaries are able to take advantage of.
So, where can we compress this cycle and get it more into a process where we ask the commercial industry to experiment on their dime?
A lot of this has to do with private capital being interested in the defense market. They’re making a bet that they can get through some of the experimentation, and then we can follow on with prototyping and quickly get into low-rate and high-rate production before fielding.
Fielding then allows us to get immediate feedback that goes back into industry. That is essentially what had to happen in Ukraine because it’s existential to them.
So, when we say wartime footing, Ukraine is on the ultimate wartime footing, and there are lessons to draw from there. What are the unnecessary steps in the acquisition process? Where can you smartly accept risk?
Probably one of the biggest drivers of speeding things up is acknowledging that we’re willing to accept risk. We know that if we get a tighter innovation cycle, we’re accepting more risk on the battlefield, but we’re also driving down risk on the battlefield because we’re getting it to them much sooner.
So, then we get into how that translates to fires. Exquisite versus low cost. It’s a balance, or a high-low mix, essentially, where we have to have both offensive and defensive exquisite weapons.
We have to have certain stockpiles to be able to counter the exquisite weapons of our adversaries and have our own effects. Then you get into mass, which comes when we start going beyond the first few days of a conflict, and we’re in protraction. We have to have affordable mass. The cost curve needs to come back in our favor.
While balancing the above, how much of a difference has the surge in domestic manufacturing made in having these pre-positioned elements assisting efforts?
A massive difference.
The Infantry Squad Vehicle is a perfect example. That’s a Chevy Colorado chassis; the drivetrain and suspension are a little different, but it’s nothing unusual.
Essentially, it then goes to a detailer that puts the military-specific equipment on top of it. It’s everything that we need it to be.
As with anything, it has its vulnerabilities. We’re sacrificing heavy armor and survivability, which we needed throughout the GWOT years, for mobility, transportability and ease of repair.
But using this model also allows us to sustain it far more easily because so many of the components are commercial.
It especially matters when you get into keeping the ISV — or domestically made equipment — in the decades ahead and needing improvements over the years. With the ISV, as Chevy makes improvements to its chassis and drivetrain, that immediately feeds back into the production line of ISVs.
So, we’re now getting upgrades that are just byproducts of the commercial market.
With acquisition, there’s a major emphasis on AI. What are you discussing with tech companies to ensure the human-in-the-loop element equates to maintaining final say despite the speed of the tech?
Every company that deals with this emerging technology and the military is of the same mindset, which is that the human-in-the-loop factor has to be the default.
There are workflows and cycles that human commanders can say, “I need this to run in the background, and I don’t need to see it or be on it.” But when it comes to kinetic kill chains and making decisions on the battlefield, the workflows that enable commanders have to have very hard stops.
It’s not just a commander saying yes or no. It’s far more complicated and nuanced. It’s presenting options based on a tremendous amount of computing analysis and saying, “Here are all the courses of action based on the priorities that you gave, based on the environmental factors that the agents have been able to ingest and all of the long-term planning that goes into it.
That allows the commanders to then take highly complex tasks like mission planning and distill it down into areas where they can consume it more easily, and then apply what only humans can do, which is context and reason.
That context and reason part is what the tech companies that work with us are very focused on enabling, as opposed to taking over entire workflows.
Autonomy is important, really, in three areas when it comes to warfighting.
Think about combat breaching. That’s one of the most dangerous things we ask a human to do: to breach a linear minefield or barrier. If we can automate that, that removes something inherently dangerous.
The second is highly complex, like command and control. How do you distill what would take human staff officers hours or days into seconds, and give a commander not only several options, but the analysis behind it and the confidence in the product being presented?
The third is the ability to remove repetitive and mundane things human soldiers are doing. Resupplying via trucks, for instance. If we can automate that, we are removing that task from our logistics soldiers and allowing them to apply their talents to solving real problems with a clear vision and mindset.
Beyond weapon systems, something as simple as staging — or hiding — equipment or personnel requires a vastly different strategy than even 10 years ago. How does something as simple as saying, “How do we hide this helo?” impact your conversations with industry?
It’s not something that we’ve had to truly consider as an Army for 40 or 50 years because we were guaranteed air superiority.
We don’t have air superiority at this point because of long-range fires and precision targeting from space.
So, you go back to dispersion, displacement of assets and disaggregation of large headquarters. As you remember from recent decades, a division headquarters would be a massive entity with satellite dishes and other assets in the open. Those days are gone.
We now have to consider how we bring in technology from the companies to allow us to displace 10-foot satellite dishes and 20 miles of wire, and actually have small-scale edge compute and transport systems that can disaggregate everyone. That’s incredibly important.
Certainly, camouflage comes into play. Other classified capabilities come into play as well, and that’s all just the visible element. Then you get into electronic warfare and the ability to monitor.
So, how do you disaggregate some of that?
Those are all things that we are actively moving — and coming back to — in a more modern stance.
J.D. Simkins is Editor-in-Chief of Military Times and Defense News, and a Marine Corps veteran of the Iraq War.

articles.title: Mojave STOL and Gray Eagle® 25M: Complementary capabilities for the modern battlefield
articles.snippet: [Sponsored] Both aircraft are designed to evolve as threats and mission requirements change.
articles.full_text:
A new, more challenging operational environment means the U.S. Army must field platforms that generate strategic advantages while conducting missions from the tactical edge.
Today’s battlefield is contested across all domains. The proliferation of low-cost, effective systems, as well as high-tech munitions, long-range missiles, and advanced air defenses, means platforms must operate effectively in denied conditions without imposing unsustainable costs or maintenance demands.
General Atomics Aeronautical Systems, Inc. (GA-ASI) offers two aircraft tailored to the Army’s need to operate in this threat environment, with the flexibility to adapt as those needs evolve: the Mojave Short Takeoff and Landing (STOL) aircraft and the Gray Eagle® 25M.
Although the aircraft share elements of the Gray Eagle family, they are optimized for different operational challenges.
Mojave STOL is designed to deliver expeditionary access from austere locations, while Gray Eagle 25M offers the endurance and range necessary for the Pacific theater, along with the payload capacity to support the Army’s multi-domain operations concept.
Bringing Aviation Closer to the Mission
Mojave STOL is designed for missions where runways are undesirable, unavailable, damaged, or vulnerable. Its STOL capability enables operations from unimproved surfaces, including roads and dirt tracks, as well as from amphibious vessels.
Runway independence expands commanders’ options in remote or contested areas. The aircraft can operate closer to distributed forces, take on fuel and munitions at austere locations, and return to the fight without relying on airfield infrastructure.
This approach reflects an enduring operational lesson: in demanding environments, rugged, reliable, and plentiful platforms can provide an advantage over systems that are more complex, expensive, or difficult to maintain.
Mojave STOL provides options for overwhelming mass at the right time and place while retaining key sensor and payload capabilities and supporting long-range, persistent mission profiles.
While modern electric and vertical-lift concepts offer tactical flexibility, their high unit costs, mechanical complexity, undetermined supply chain security, and maintenance burdens present challenges for sustained expeditionary operations driving cost, manpower, and risk.
Mojave STOL is built around a straightforward, time-tested aircraft, a proven design, and an established production and sustainment philosophy, enabling the flexibility to move with expeditionary forces while avoiding complex infrastructure demands.
Its ability to operate from smaller naval vessels also creates potential applications for maritime, contested logistics, and special operations missions.
Modernizing Gray Eagle for Contested Operations
Gray Eagle 25M is an extensively modernized version of the MQ-1C Gray Eagle, designed to support long-endurance missions in complex threat environments. Its roles include persistent, real-time threat detection/identification and support for long-range targeting operations.
A central feature of the aircraft is its Modular Open Systems Approach (MOSA) architecture.
MOSA uses defined interfaces and modular components to help integrate new technologies more quickly and affordably. This open architecture approach is intended to help the Army respond to changing threats while reducing the time and cost associated with future upgrades.
Another significant improvement comes in the form of the expeditionary laptop-based ground control station and ground support equipment. This portable system eliminates the need for large, containerized GCS satellite systems, transport vehicles, and ground support equipment, reducing equipment weight by 130,000 pounds per platoon.
Combined with the new, more powerful turbo-diesel Heavy Fuel Engine (HFE) 2.0, these improvements reduce field service representative and soldier workload while increasing maintenance-free operational periods, with a sustainment cost savings of roughly $200 million annually.
The EagleEye® multi-mode radar, for example, is designed to provide substantially greater range than legacy systems, with an increase of up to five times.
Together, these capabilities support Gray Eagle 25M’s mission to maintain persistent awareness and contribute to decision-making in high-threat environments.
Complementary Aircraft for the Army
The two aircraft offer the Army a complementary range of capabilities.
Mojave STOL is optimized for expeditionary access, operational flexibility, and runway-independent operations in regions such as the Indo-Pacific, where forces cannot count on reliable access to paved runways.
Gray Eagle 25M is optimized for endurance, sensing, processing, and survivability in contested environments. Its advanced sensor suite, combined with tactics refined through millions of hours of combat operations by Gray Eagle and other GA-ASI aircraft, enables the platform to operate over long distances and remain effective in high-threat conditions.
Both aircraft are designed to evolve as threats and mission requirements change.
Gray Eagle 25M and Mojave’s open architecture support the integration of new capabilities, helping maintain relevance across different areas of operation. What’s more, they cover the full breadth of conflict, from peacetime to large-scale combat operations, with adaptable, responsive, critical capability.
Mojave STOL can likewise accommodate expanded payload options, including electronic warfare systems and air-launched effects.
Investing in Scalable Capability
GA-ASI has made manufacturing and engineering investments intended to support continued modernization and larger-scale production.
Collaboration with Hanwha Aerospace is expanding production facilities and research and development activities, helping create the infrastructure needed to support scalable output.
The partnership is aimed at advancing Mojave STOL’s capabilities while supporting more affordable production. That means the Army will not necessarily have to choose between capability and mass.
In addition, GA-ASI’s existing millions of square feet of manufacturing infrastructure, skilled in-house workforce, and available capacity position the company to begin building and delivering aircraft today.
By choosing Gray Eagle 25M and Mojave STOL, the Army would be investing in mature, adaptable capabilities designed for rapid delivery and scalable employment.
Visitors to GA-ASI’s Booth 6619 at the Association of the United States Army’s Annual Meeting and Exposition can discuss with experts how these systems are prepared to support Army operations in today’s high-threat environments and adapt to the challenges ahead.

articles.title: Amid unease in Europe, NATO SACEUR bullish on ‘block, blunt, break’ theory of victory
articles.snippet: “I want others to know who might be thinking about doing harm against us, that we’ve got this, and that they better not take any shot at the alliance,” said Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, who also serves as commander of United States European Command.
articles.full_text:
BELFAST — Despite assuring an audience today that a conflict on NATO territory is neither “imminent or inevitable,” Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, the alliance’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe, outlined a strategic “theory of victory” and offered a warning to potential aggressors.
He told the Warsaw Security Forum that NATO’s aim is to deter adversaries, “but if someone is foolish enough to attack us, we will fight,” adding that “any attack against any ally” will end up “utterly futile.”
NATO is capable of carrying out this vision by implementing its “theory of victory,” a classified version of which was agreed upon by all 32 alliance members “about three months ago,” according to Grynkewich.
Grynkewich, who also serves as commander of United States European Command, did not say against whom, exactly, the alliance would fight, but the speech comes as European capitals have increasingly called out Russia for what they alleged are a string of sabotage cases across the continent. Grynkewich said the incidents were making allied populations “a bit nervous.”
“What I want to do is assure the one billion citizens of the alliance that we’ve got this. We know what we need to do,” he said.
Grynkewich warned, “I want others to know who might be thinking about doing harm against us, that we’ve got this, and that they better not take any shot at the alliance.”
The theory of victory is structured around blocking, blunting and breaking an enemy — beginning with stymieing an initial attack and preventing an enemy advance by weakening it. Drawing on the final part of the theory, said Grynkewich, “we will break the enemy’s forces and the operational warfighting system that is arrayed against us.”
Concentrating more on the warfighting elements to execute the new doctrine, he noted the “synchronized employment of multi-domain effects down to the tactical level” in order to “overwhelm enemy formations in contact.”
The end result would see enemy forces degraded to such an extent that they would be unable to continue an attack, explained Grynkewich.
“Across the alliance, we’re taking steps to operationalize this theory and maximize the readiness of our forces,” he made clear. “If attacked, we are ready to fight tonight.”
Grynkewich’s comments come as Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski warned today that NATO allies must be prepared to deal with a deadly Russian hybrid attack.
Separately, when assessing the state of the Ukraine war, Grynkewich noted that the frontline has “largely stabilized” and that Russian long range attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, “probably” won’t break the will of the country’s civilian population.

articles.title: CHAOS Industries joins low-cost interceptor parade with VESPID design
articles.snippet: The system comes in two sizes: man-portable Mk 0, and the vehicle-launched Mk 1.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — Defense tech startup CHAOS Industries has unveiled a new family of small low-cost interceptors, dubbed VESPID.
The system comes in two sizes: the Mk 0, which is “man-portable and designed for austere environments,” and the Mk 1, which is “a faster, more maneuverable variant designed for high-density installations with a multitube launcher,” according to a company press release.
That multitube launcher is an existing system from ISS Aerospace, a UK company, according to a company spokesperson, who added that the Mk 1 can be integrated with Coyote launchers as well. That’s notable, as integration with Coyote is a key requirement for the Army’s Next Generation C-sUAS Missile program, which the service launched in August.
The spokesperson said that while the firm is not under contract at this time with any militaries, “We are participating in several domestic and international competitions with both Mk 0 and Mk 1 variants.”
The press release also highlights an “[a]bility to operate in congested electromagnetic environments.” According to the spokesperson, that line is in reference to a plan to use CHAOS’s radar transmitter “as a datalink to burn through jamming. In addition, the datalink waveform contains means for error detection and correction.”
Production wise, CHAOS claims plans are in place for a production capacity of 12,000 interceptors per year, with “a manufacturing architecture capable of expanding to 50,000” as needed. Work would be done at the company’s recently opened El Segundo, Calif. location.
The Los Angeles-based firm, which launched in 2022, becomes one of many to roll out new missile defense systems during this year’s AUSA conference, including low-cost interceptors from Anduril and Lockheed Martin, and a host of c-UAS radars and EW systems on the show floor.

articles.title: Acting army secretary announces ‘manufacturing rodeo’ to tackle ‘weak links’ in supply chain
articles.snippet: “The magic is that this is an early indicator that we’re acquiring a new system of seamless, frictionless symbiosis between the Army and American commercial excellence,” said Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle today announced the service will hold an event aimed at finding weak spots in the service’s supply chain, which the service is calling a “manufacturing rodeo.”
“We need to make the things we need here in America, and to keep making them when demand surges. That’s why I’m announcing today that the US Army is going to do something we’ve never done before,” Telle said today at the annual AUSA conference, marking his largest address to soldiers and industry since taking on the acting secretary role.
“Early next year, we will conduct what I’m calling a manufacturing rodeo, a race between our industrial base partners.”
Telle did not divulge many details about the upcoming event, but said since the Army has invested “a lot in our organic industrial base,” the service will now hold a competition of sorts between industry where they will “strain” and “stress test” the supply chain to “see where it breaks.”
“The magic is that this is an early indicator that we’re acquiring a new system of seamless, frictionless symbiosis between the Army and American commercial excellence,” Telle said. “We built those muscles in World War II, but we haven’t flexed them since the Cold War, and as I said, the script has flipped. Take a basic attack drone. We need to be able to make millions of these. It may look simple, but it’s a flying supply chain we don’t control enough of.”
Though Telle said the Army is focused on modernization efforts such as bolstering its supply chain, he also wants to put an increased emphasis on getting “back to the basics.”
“I’m going to take it back to the basics, back to the dirt that lies beneath that foundation, because government agencies are in such a race trying to one up each other on the path to technocratic superiority that we often blow right past the fundamentals,” Telle said. “We’re so eager to talk about how we’re playing with the shiniest, newest, most headline-worthy gadgets that we forget what we were trying to do in the first place.”
Getting back to the basics includes focusing on “controlling and securing land,” Telle said.
“[C]ontrolling land is fundamental to humanity. The Army does it better than anyone, and it’s on us, the people in this room, to keep it that way. Humanity’s connection to the land is biblical, and it even transcends faith.”

articles.title: Mine hunting goes remote as the Navy replaces minesweepers with robots
articles.snippet: With minesweepers retired, the US is turning to remote and robotic mine-neutralization tactics.
articles.full_text:
Maritime mines are a concern for the US and its allies in a number of regions, including the Strait of Hormuz and the South China Sea. In addition to being a threat to military vessels, mines can slow or halt commercial traffic through important trade and oil routes.
Breaking Defense spoke with Bryan Clark, director of the Hudson Institute’s Center for Defense Concepts and Technology, on the threat of mines, how they can be neutralized and the role of remote mine hunting in keeping personnel out of harm’s way.
Breaking Defense: Why are maritime mines such a serious threat in some of these strategic choke points like the Strait of Hormuz or the South China Sea?
Clark: Partly because they’re so easy to obtain or build, and then deploy. The Iranians even have rockets that can deploy mines at a standoff distance into the strait. That’s just an example of how easy it is to put these mines out there because you don’t need to precision guide them. You just drop them into the approximate area of the channel and that’s going to be sufficient to hold up traffic.
Mines don’t have to be sophisticated. There are obviously very sophisticated ones that look for particular acoustic or magnetic signatures. There are some that’ll measure how many ships go across and detonate on the third or fourth ship, but they don’t need to be smart in order to be effective. All you need is somebody to detect the mine and know that it’s there, and it’s going to cause vessel traffic to stop until the mine threat has been eliminated.
The barrier to entry is low. Countries can easily field a capable mine-laying capability or mine-laying force and then deny access in a critical strait or choke point. You have countries out there for whom mines are the main weapon, like Finland. When they think about having to face off against the Russians, the first thing they plan on doing is mining the Gulf of Finland, which prevents access to and from Sevastopol or St. Petersburg. You’ve cut off one of Russia’s only warm water ports by closing off the Gulf of Finland, and that’s for them their primary offensive capability.
For Iran, obviously the drone revolution has given them another offensive weapon, but mines have always been one of their main go-tos in terms of offensive weapons. It’s always been perceived that they would try to use them to close off the Strait of Hormuz because it is such a narrow choke point and so vital to global commerce.
The other thing about mines that makes them more potent as a threat is that you’d only need the threat of a mine in order to close off access. If you have a mine detection or even a concern about mines, vessel traffic will generally stop until the threat’s been verified or validated, or shipping companies decide to accept the risk and either pay higher insurance rates or accept the potential loss of their own ship. It’ll impact shipping even if you just have the threat of a mine without the physical presence of them. That makes them an effective tool even for small countries.
How do you determine if a mine is a valid threat?
You can’t discount the threat. Because shipping companies don’t want to accept the risk of them being wrong or you being wrong if you say, ‘there’s not really a mine threat’ You have to take it at face value.
The first thing you do is find a channel that’s mine-free. That’s what the US did early on in the war. They used the remote-mine hunting systems they had to verify that the channel along the Omani coast was free of mines. Once you’ve verified a channel free of mines, it doesn’t necessarily matter that there might be mines elsewhere. You can lead ships through that safe passage, and then if you want to increase traffic or provide for more two-way traffic, then you have to expand the channel and search a larger area.
How does the Navy currently hunt and neutralize mines, and how has that task become less dangerous?
It used to be very dangerous, because you’d have to send a human-operated minesweeper out, which puts people at risk. Mine-hunting ships have been traditionally wooden or fiberglass to avoid creating a magnetic signature. They use a sonar system on the front to detect the mines and then they will have a sweep system they tow on the back or they’ll use neutralization systems to neutralize the mines after they find them.
Now the systems they use are robots. They have active sonars on board that they use to search for mines. It becomes kind of like a Roomba, where the robots go up and down the route looking for mines in the water column. They’ll stay near the surface and then look down into the water, and as long as the water is not extremely deep, they’ll be able to see the first 100 or 200 feet of water and detect mine-like objects.
They’ll identify things that they think are mines. When they do their run and come back, you download all the data off of them into a computer, which has processing software that helps you to figure out what are things that need further investigation.
Then you can send out another set of robots to investigate the things that might be mines to get a better idea of whether they’re really mines or if they were objects dumped on the seafloor or, things floating in the water that aren’t mines. That usually narrows down how many things you have to investigate further.
At the point you’ve determined there’s mine or mine-like objects in the water that have to be neutralized, you then send out a helicopter or a small boat with a mine neutralization system on it, which is a floating vehicle that has little torpedoes that’ll come off of it and those are fiber-optically guided to the target. You have a video screen and a joystick, and you steer those mine neutralizers to the mine and they detonate on that object.
Either they blow up the mine – if it’s a mine – or they punch a hole in it and it sinks to the bottom. These mine neutralizers have been around for 20 years or so, but they do keep the people out of the minefield.
It keeps people out of the minefield because now you don’t have to have the minesweeper driving into the minefield anymore. You can also do it at a greater scale. Because I can buy a lot more robots than I can buy minesweepers, because every minesweeper needs a crew and people are expensive. If you want to expand your mine-hunting fleet, you end up having to buy a bunch of manned ships. If you’re buying robots instead, you can buy a bunch of robots, store them, and then bring them out when you need to do the mine-hunting operation.
As you look forward, what do you see as the capabilities that will be needed most for counter-mine operations?
Onboard processing and communications. One of the limitations of the current way of doing it is you have to have the vessels or the vehicles doing the mine hunting come back and download all their data, then analyze it and then send out another set of vehicles to go investigate the likely mine areas to verify, and then send out another set of vehicles to go do the mine neutralization – helicopters and small boats with mine-neutralization systems. It’s a multi-pass setup the way it is now.
If instead you had onboard processing from these mine-hunting vehicles, the underwater vehicles looking for the mines could come up and transmit data back to you immediately and say, ‘I finished path one. I found a bunch of mines or potential mines. They’re here.’ Then you can quickly decide whether to send another vehicle out there right now to investigate, or to just send the mine neutralization system out immediately.
You should be able to get to a point where you can do this in a way that is just robot after robot after robot.

articles.title: AGVs vs. UGVs: A new class of ground autonomy takes the field
articles.snippet: [Sponsored] One commander, many robots: Fully autonomous ground vehicles are reshaping the battlefield.
articles.full_text:
Ground robots have proven their value in recent conflicts, handling logistics runs, evacuating the wounded, and keeping troops away from the most dangerous environments. But unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) have a critical limitation: they aren’t fully autonomous. UGVs are remote-controlled or teleoperated, tethered to a communications link that can be jammed, spoofed, or severed. They also require the full attention of their human operator, which is cognitively expensive.
Overland AI’s fully autonomous ground vehicles (AGVs) represent a significant advancement over UGVs.
Leveraging proprietary software and hardware, Overland AI’s AGVs can sense and navigate the world around them independently, overcoming obstacles such as boulders, dense vegetation, steep slopes, and unexpected ditches at tactically relevant speeds. They can do this even when signals are degraded or lost entirely. Using natural language prompts, a single operator can task and orchestrate an entire fleet of these AGVs simultaneously—without teleoperation or remote control.
Overland AI’s technology has been refined and validated through rigorous field testing and extensive work with warfighters. In a joint U.S. military exercise in Africa this year, Army officers estimated that two AGVs replaced 40 humans, allowing troops to move faster with more protection. The vehicles reduced distribution time on a drop zone by 52 percent at another recent military event. During breaching, one of the most dangerous tasks for troops, service members face extreme casualty rates. When fully autonomous vehicles are deployed, humans are removed from the most dangerous places on the battlefield, life expectancy skyrockets, and more U.S. troops can return home to their families.
Overland AI recently became the first ground autonomy company to prime a production contract for the U.S. military. Under a $20 million agreement through the Accelerate the Procurement and Fielding of Innovative Technologies (APFIT) program, the company is working with the U.S. Marine Corps to produce and field AGVs in support of the Marine Air Defense Integrated System (MADIS).
The APFIT award is the culmination of a push within the Department of War to move autonomous systems into programs of record and operational use. Missions such as breaching fortified positions, delivering critical supplies under fire, and detecting and defeating enemy drones are ready for autonomous deployment.
Truly autonomous ground vehicles are not a future capability—they are operational now. This is important because however the battlefield evolves, wars are still won on the ground. Territory must be taken, held, and defended by forces operating across austere environments marked by uncertain conditions and degraded communications.
The robotics revolution in land warfare is here, and Overland AI is driving it. The next step is fielding this technology broadly across the services.

articles.title: Ukraine strikes third Yandex data center, disrupting digital services across Russia
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: A third Yandex data center in Russia was hit by Ukrainian drones over the weekend, forcing it to shut down and causing further disruptions to cloud services, payments, deliveries and other online services across the country.
articles.full_text:
Ukraine strikes third Yandex data center, disrupting digital services across Russia
A third Yandex data center in Russia was hit by Ukrainian drones over the weekend, forcing it to shut down and causing further disruptions to cloud services, payments, deliveries and other online services across the country.
The latest attack, overnight Sunday, targeted a Yandex facility in Vladimir, following strikes on two other data centers in the Ryazan and Kaluga regions earlier last week.
“The data center has shut down completely, and the remaining infrastructure is unstable. The platform is operating in emergency mode,” Yandex said in a statement.
Over the past week, Ukrainian drones targeted three of Yandex's six data centers in Russia, forcing two facilities to shut down completely and damaging infrastructure at the third.
The first attack occurred overnight October 7-8, when drones struck a Yandex data center in Sasovo, in the Ryazan region, sparking a fire and forcing the company to shut down the facility. The site, which opened in 2014, reportedly houses two of Yandex's three supercomputers used to train artificial intelligence models.
A second strike hit a data center in Kaluga on October 9, damaging part of its infrastructure. Yandex said no employees were injured and emergency responders were working at the site. The third facility, targeted over the weekend in Vladimir, houses Galushkin, another Yandex supercomputer considered among the most powerful in Russia. Yandex has not disclosed whether any of its supercomputers were damaged in the attacks.
The three targeted facilities have a combined capacity of approximately 115 megawatts.
Widespread impact
The attacks have disrupted Yandex Cloud, which provides computing infrastructure to thousands of businesses, as well as some of the company's own services and third-party platforms that depend on its servers.
According to the Russian internet watchdog, users have experienced problems accessing email, booking taxis, ordering food and making payments through Yandex Pay. The company's Alice voice assistant and connected smart home devices have also reportedly stopped working in some households.
More than a dozen third-party services hosted on Yandex infrastructure were also reportedly affected, including retailers, internet providers, an online psychotherapy service, fitness businesses and the Russian segment of TikTok.
The full extent of the disruptions remains unclear. Yandex Cloud served approximately 64,000 customers as of mid-2026, according to the company's financial disclosures, but Yandex has not revealed how many were affected by the attacks.
Following the latest strike, the company advised cloud customers to consider alternative recovery plans rather than relying solely on switching between parts of Yandex Cloud's own infrastructure
Russian state media reported that Yandex had reached agreements with competing cloud providers Selectel, K2Cloud and VK Cloud to help affected customers move their data and services more quickly.
Retaliatory attack
In a statement Friday, Yandex described its data centers as the “iron heart” of the company and acknowledged the widespread impact of the outages.
“Every outage means disrupted plans and an inability to do things that are part of everyday life or work,” the company said. “At this point, it is very difficult to provide a timeline for restoring the equipment at the data centers.”
On Saturday, Yandex also updated its terms of service to exclude liability for failing to meet contractual obligations because of drone strikes and other attacks, potentially limiting customers' ability to seek compensation for disruptions.
The attacks have prompted discussions within the Russian government about strengthening protection for the country's digital infrastructure.
Russian Digital Development Minister Maksut Shadayev said his ministry was working with the Defense Ministry on measures to improve security at Yandex facilities.
“Yandex has faced an unprecedented attack. We are discussing how to protect these facilities,” Shadayev added.
The strikes come after Russian attacks damaged several Ukrainian data centers and telecommunications facilities in late September, disrupting internet access for thousands of households.
At least six Ukrainian data centers, including facilities operated by MiroHost, Parkovy, Data Group, Utels and Pautina, were damaged. Infrastructure belonging to major telecommunications providers Kyivstar and Ukrtelecom was also hit.
A Russian strike on September 23 disrupted fixed-line internet access for approximately 100,000 households in Kyiv and the surrounding region, according to Ukrainian officials.
Moscow has claimed that Ukrainian data centers were being used to support the country's armed forces.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky last week acknowledged attacks on data centers in Russia, describing them as retaliation for Russian strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure.
“We always respond in kind. You all know that they have attacked and continue to attack our data centers. We responded,” Zelensky told reporters.
Daryna Antoniuk
is a reporter for Recorded Future News based in Ukraine. She writes about cybersecurity startups, cyberattacks in Eastern Europe and the state of the cyberwar between Ukraine and Russia. She previously was a tech reporter for Forbes Ukraine. Her work has also been published at Sifted, The Kyiv Independent and The Kyiv Post.

articles.title: Cyberattack disrupts refrigeration at hundreds of French supermarkets
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: A cyberattack overnight Sunday disrupted refrigerators at hundreds of French supermarkets, spoiling fresh food at stores run by some of the country’s largest grocery chains.
articles.full_text:
Cyberattack disrupts refrigeration at hundreds of French supermarkets
A cyberattack overnight Sunday disrupted refrigerators at hundreds of French supermarkets, according to retailers and French media.
Fresh food spoiled at stores run by some of the country’s largest grocery chains after attackers remotely triggered the units’ defrost function.
French broadcaster BFMTV reported that about 300 Intermarché and Netto stores and fewer than 100 Coopérative U stores were affected.
“I confirm that a cyberattack has been affecting, since last night, the cold production facilities of several stores in our network” said the Coopérative U chief executive Dominique Schelcher.
“Our teams are fully mobilized, in coordination with refrigeration specialists, to restore the situation as quickly as possible,” he added.
“Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is of extreme gravity and is unprecedented,” said Schelcher. “It is unacceptable.”
France’s national cybersecurity agency, ANSSI, said in an emailed statement that it was “mobilised to handle this incident” both at the national level to support potential victims and at the European level to coordinate with its counterparts.
BFMTV reported that the affected systems are refrigeration controllers made by Danish manufacturer Danfoss, and that the attackers targeted older versions of its software.
Groupement Mousquetaires, which owns Intermarché and Netto, said the affected systems were managed by Danfoss, Bloomberg reported. The group said it would be up to the supplier to file a criminal complaint.
Danfoss has not publicly confirmed that its systems were the target, and a spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Security researchers have previously flagged weaknesses in Danfoss refrigeration controllers. Last year, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency published an advisory regarding three of these vulnerabilities.
Researchers at Claroty’s Team82 later showed that a compromised controller could switch off cooling while still reporting normal temperatures to staff. They counted more than 2,700 of the devices exposed to the internet. It is not known whether those flaws were used in Sunday’s attack.
Alexander Martin
is the UK Editor for Recorded Future News. He was previously a technology reporter for Sky News and a fellow at the European Cyber Conflict Research Initiative, now Virtual Routes. He can be reached securely using Signal on: AlexanderMartin.79

articles.title: Cyberattack shuts down refrigerators at French supermarkets
articles.snippet: Attackers remotely defrosted refrigerators at multiple French supermarket chains overnight in a cyberattack that reportedly targeted Danfoss refrigeration controllers. [...]
articles.full_text:
Attackers remotely defrosted refrigerators at multiple French supermarket chains overnight in a cyberattack that reportedly targeted Danfoss refrigeration controllers.
Victims include Intermarché, Coopérative U, Carrefour Market, Monoprix, Leclerc, and Super U, with French outlets reporting that the attack affected 250 to 350 stores, causing significant financial losses and food waste.
The threat actors hijacked refrigeration controllers running older versions of Danfoss control software on Sunday night and used them to raise supermarket refrigerator temperatures by triggering a built-in automatic defrosting system.
"Following a cyberattack reportedly affecting a service provider that manages refrigeration systems in stores, some fresh and frozen food display units are out of service," an Intermarché spokesperson told BleepingComputer when asked for more information on the incident. "Intermarché and Netto have taken all necessary precautions to remove the products from these units as quickly as possible. We don't have further information currently, nor a specific list of affected stores to share with you."
Coopérative U president Dominique Schelcher also confirmed the incident earlier today and said that the attack affected multiple stores in the chain.
"I can confirm that, since last night, a cyberattack has been affecting the refrigeration systems in several stores within our @CooperativeU network. Our teams are fully mobilized, working alongside refrigeration specialists, to resolve the situation as quickly as possible. An investigation will be conducted to shed full light on this attack," Schelcher said.
"Targeting equipment essential for preserving fresh produce and supplying food to the French people is an extremely serious matter and is unprecedented. It is unacceptable."
EU agriculture and food commissioner Christophe Hansen also condemned the attack and named France's largest supermarket chain, Leclerc, as one of the victims.
The Paris prosecutor's office has told AFP that it has opened an investigation into "the large-scale cyberattack affecting the refrigerators of several major food retail chains across France" to "identify the victims and establish the link with the damage they reported in terms of foodstuff losses and the outbreak of fires."
While no information is available on how the Danfoss refrigeration controllers were compromised, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) warned in May 2025 of an authentication bypass vulnerability (CVE-2025-41450) and in August 2025 of a command injection flaw (CVE-2025-41451) in the Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA Series hardware platform used to manage refrigeration and HVAC systems typically found in the food retail sector.
Claroty's Team82 research team, which found the two flaws, also published a detailed write-up in August on how they can be exploited to achieve remote code execution on Danfoss AK-SM 800A publicly accessible management interfaces.
While researching the attack surface, Predicta Lab CEO Baptiste Robert found 2752 Danfoss systems exposed online on Monday, 1590 of them in France. Shodan, a search engine for Internet-connected devices, is also tracking over 4,500 Danfoss devices reachable over the Internet.
Spokespersons for Danfoss, Leclerc, and Coopérative U were not immediately available for comment when contacted by BleepingComputer earlier today.
Although there is no evidence yet that the two are connected, retail giant Ahold Delhaize, one of the world's largest food retail chains, also announced on Monday that it had to take some systems offline after a "cybersecurity incident."
